title: The small catechism
hookLine: Luther wrote a simple Q&A for families: what does this mean?

lines: A BOOKLET ON THE TABLE AT HOME.
NOT A THICKER BOOK. A THINNER ONE.
cards: A small booklet, open on a table at home. A parent reads a line out loud: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Then comes the question the booklet asks after almost every line: what does this mean?
And a child answers, in a sentence short enough to remember. That's the scene Martin Luther wrote for.

In the preface to his Small Catechism, he describes going around the parishes and being shocked at what he found: ordinary people who barely knew the Lord's Prayer or the commandments, and pastors who couldn't teach them.
His answer wasn't a thicker book. It was a thinner one.

teach.h: A TEACHING BOOK FOR THE HOUSEHOLD.
teach.b: A catechism is a teaching book, usually in questions and answers, for learning the basics of the faith. Luther also wrote a larger one for pastors.
The small one has a note at the top of each part: this is how the head of a household should teach it, simply, to the family. So the classroom he had in mind was a home.

It walks through the Ten Commandments, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer, then baptism, confession and the Lord's Supper. After each piece comes the same short question: what does this mean? The answers are plain.

teach.h: FEAR, LOVE AND TRUST ABOVE ALL.
teach.b: The first commandment, no other gods: in Luther's answer, we should fear, love and trust God above all things. One breath.
Or take the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." What does daily bread mean? Luther's answer sounds like a household inventory.

It includes food and drink, clothing and shoes, house and home, fields and cattle, money and goods, a faithful spouse, good government, good weather, peace, health, good friends and faithful neighbors, and the like.

Shoes and good weather, inside the Lord's Prayer. The question does something on its own, too. It assumes words you've said over and over might still be closed to you, and it invites you to open them.

Lutheran churches still teach with it. Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed Christians have catechisms of their own, each with its own questions and answers. But Luther's small question is one anyone can borrow.

how: Lutheran churches use Luther's Small Catechism to teach children and adults, especially before confirmation; Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches teach with catechisms of their own.

games.q: you're Luther. you've visited the parishes and found people who barely know the Lord's Prayer, and pastors who can't teach it. what do you write?
o: a long scholarly book of theology.
a small question-and-answer booklet for families.
an order that sermons must run longer.
games.why: he wrote the Small Catechism, a thin book meant to be taught at home, asking after each line: what does this mean?

practice: Choose one line you've said so often it slides past: a line of the Lord's Prayer, a blessing before meals, a saying a grandparent used to repeat.
Say it once, slowly, then ask the catechism's question and answer it in one plain sentence of your own. If you pray, end by saying the line again as a prayer; if not, let your sentence sit.
